issues.legal_issue: A scaled map clearly demarcating a boundary and incorporated into a lease governs the boundary and cannot be displaced by reconstructing it from revenue records.
material_facts: The adjoining leaseholders disputed whether the encroached coal land lay within one leasehold or the other.
A later lease in the respondents’ chain of title included a map drawn to scale that clearly marked the boundary between the leaseholds.
Subleases in the appellants’ chain of title also referred to maps showing the same boundary line, and the appellants did not produce a map referred to in their predecessor’s lease.
The disputed land lay within the boundary shown on the map accepted by the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The map incorporated into the lease governed the boundary; it was not permissible to reconstruct that boundary by reference to revenue records, and the disputed land was part of the respondents’ holding.
issues.legal_principle: A map referred to in a lease is incorporated into and forms part of the lease. Where that map is drawn to scale and clearly demarcates the boundary, the court may not ignore it and reconstruct the boundary by reference to revenue records. The Court relied on Darapali Sadagar v. Najir Ahamed (1923) I.L.R. 50 Cal. 394.

predicates.boundary_dispute_between_adjacent_leaseh: The parties to the land dispute hold adjoining leaseholds with a disputed dividing boundary.
predicates.lease_incorporates_boundary_map: A lease relevant to the boundary refers to a map as part of the lease.
predicates.map_is_scaled_and_clearly_demarcates_bou: The incorporated map is drawn to scale and clearly marks the boundary.
predicates.disputed_land_is_within_the_boundary_sho: The disputed land falls on the side of the boundary shown by the incorporated map that belongs to the claimant.

issues.definition: When adjoining leaseholders dispute a boundary, a scaled and clear boundary map incorporated into a lease determines which leasehold contains the disputed land.

issues.legal_issue: In a claim governed by a limitation period that begins when the claimant first learns whose possession the property is in, the claimant bears the constant legal burden of establishing that the claim is within time, although the evidentiary onus may shift.
material_facts: The respondents sought relief concerning coal allegedly taken from their land and alleged that they first learned of the encroachment and removal after receiving information from the Mines Department in 1941.
The appellants alleged that the respondents had knowledge of the encroachment from a 1932 survey.
The respondents’ colliery manager testified that he first learned of the encroachment in 1941 and denied earlier knowledge.
The courts accepted that testimony and found that the 1932 materials did not establish the respondents’ knowledge of the encroachment or removal of coal.
The appellants provided no acceptable evidence that the respondents had learned of the relevant possession more than three years before filing suit.
issues.conclusion: The initial legal burden was on the respondents to establish that the suit was within time, and the High Court’s finding was not vitiated by placing that burden on the appellants; the accepted evidence established knowledge within the limitation period, so the suit was not barred.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 48 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, the limitation period for the relevant claim ran from when the person entitled to possession first learned whose possession the property was in. Because that date was within the claimant’s special knowledge, the claimant had the initial burden of proving it. Section 3 of that Act required the court to dismiss a time-barred suit even if limitation was not pleaded, and section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, placed the constant legal burden on the party asserting the facts necessary for a decision in its favour; the evidentiary onus could nevertheless shift as evidence or presumptions arose. The Court relied on Lalchand Marwari v. Mahant Rampur Gir (1925) I.L.R. 5 Pat. 312, Rajah Sahib Perhlad Sein v. Maharajah Rajender Kishore Singh (1869) 12 M.I.A. 292, Kalyani Prasad Singh v. Borrea Coal Co. Ltd. (A.I.R. 1946 Cal. 123), Bank of Bombay v. Fazulbhoy Ebrahim ((1922) 24 Bom. L.R. 513), and Talyarkhan v. Gangadas ((1935) I.L.R. 60 Bom. 848). It disapproved Sundarji Shivji v. Secretary of State for India ((1934) I.L.R. 13 Pat. 752).

predicates.claim_under_knowledge_triggered_limitati: The proceeding is a claim for recovery or compensation for property wrongfully taken or held, with the limitation period depending on when the claimant first learned whose possession it was in.
predicates.claimant_asserts_that_knowledge_arose_wi: The claimant asserts that the relevant knowledge arose within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.claimant_bears_the_constant_legal_burden: The claimant retains the legal burden of establishing that the claim was brought within time, even though the evidentiary onus may shift during the proceeding.

issues.definition: For a claim subject to knowledge-triggered limitation, a claimant asserting timely knowledge must establish that the claim was brought within time.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent finding that coal remaining in an encroached area was inaccessible and lost to its owner need not be disturbed on the basis of a possible exemption that was not raised before the lower courts.
material_facts: The respondents alleged that a required barrier made the coal remaining in the encroached area inaccessible and permanently unworkable.
The appellants did not deny that the remaining coal was lost to the respondents, but argued that the respondents might obtain an exemption from the barrier requirement and recover it.
The exemption argument had not been raised before either lower court.
Both lower courts found that the remaining coal was rendered unworkable and lost to the respondents.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the concurrent finding that the remaining coal was lost to the respondents and declined to alter it on the basis of the unraised possibility of an exemption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the concurrent factual finding that the coal was unworkable and would not decide against it on the basis of a merely possible exemption that had not been raised below. The argument concerned rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946.

predicates.claim_for_loss_of_remaining_coal: The claimant seeks relief for coal remaining in the disputed area that is said to be inaccessible.
predicates.defendant_does_not_deny_its_inaccessibil: The defendant does not deny that the remaining coal is lost or inaccessible to the claimant.
predicates.lower_courts_concurrently_find_it_unwork: Both lower courts find that the remaining coal cannot be worked by the claimant.
predicates.possible_exemption_not_raised_below: The defendant relies on a possible exemption from the restriction, but did not raise that possibility before the lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_finding_that_remaining_coal_i: The concurrent finding that the remaining coal is lost to the claimant is left undisturbed.

issues.definition: When both lower courts find remaining coal unworkable, the finding is upheld where its inaccessibility is not denied and the proposed exemption was not raised below.
